questions.q: Why does giving a model tool-calling access change the security problem compared to a model that only generates text?
options: A model's output can trigger a real action — sending an email, modifying a record, executing code — so a wrong or manipulated decision can cause real-world damage, not just an incorrect answer
Tool-calling access makes a model immune to prompt injection
It does not change anything, since tools and text generation carry identical risk
Tool-calling access only matters for models that generate images
questions.explain: Once output can trigger a real action instead of just being displayed, the cost of the model being wrong or successfully prompt-injected changes from 'it said something incorrect' to 'it did something' — potentially irreversible.

questions.q: What does 'blast radius' mean when applied to an AI agent?
options: The physical distance a server room's fire-suppression system needs to cover
The number of users who can send requests to the agent simultaneously
The worst-case damage the agent can cause if a given decision is wrong or successfully manipulated, given the access it currently holds
How many different tools an agent has been given access to, regardless of what they do
questions.explain: Blast radius reframes the question from 'could the agent be tricked' to 'if it is tricked or simply wrong, what's the worst it can do with the access it currently holds' — the right way to size agent risk.

questions.q: Why should individual tools be scoped with their own minimum credential, rather than the agent holding one broad credential shared across all its tools?
options: Because a shared broad credential is always faster to issue than scoped ones
Because scoping per tool means a prompt-injection attack that misuses one tool still can't reach further than that tool's narrow permission, limiting the blast radius
Because tool scoping has no effect on blast radius
Because broad credentials are required by most cloud providers for any agent to function
questions.explain: A read-only lookup tool should use a narrowly scoped credential, and a refund tool a separately scoped one limited to its specific job — so a successful manipulation of one tool is contained rather than reaching everything the agent could otherwise touch.

questions.q: How should the line be drawn between actions an agent can take fully autonomously and actions requiring a human approval gate?
options: No agent action should ever require human approval, since that defeats the purpose of automation
All agent actions should require approval, including simple read-only lookups
The line should be discovered only after an incident occurs, as a post-mortem exercise

Low-risk, reversible, read-only actions can run autonomously; higher-risk, hard-to-reverse, or financially/operationally significant actions belong behind a human approval gate, decided deliberately tool by tool
questions.explain: This mirrors the SOAR playbook approval-gate pattern from Course 10: the agent proposes a high-risk action and a human confirms before it executes, while low-risk reversible actions can run without that gate.

questions.q: Why is a narrow, parameterized tool schema — such as issue_refund(order_id, amount) — considered a security control rather than just an API design choice?
options: It constrains what the model can even request, unlike a general-purpose tool such as 'run this shell command,' which hands the model an unlimited capability with no structural limit
Parameterized functions always run faster than general-purpose commands
Narrow schemas eliminate the need to log tool calls
A narrow schema guarantees the model can never make a mistake when calling that tool
questions.explain: A specific, validated function limits the model to the parameters it was given, structurally bounding what it can request — a general-purpose execution tool erases most of the benefit of carefully scoping credentials in the first place.
